units:
I moved here from Busan eight months ago and I'm writing in English to practice. I wrote this haiku:
Snow in a new town—
I practice my name aloud
until it sounds mine
Please tell me what you think, and about my English too.

I'm a freelance designer and invoice clients in installments. This shows what each client still owes. I aggregated billed and paid separately first so the joins don't multiply rows:
WITH b AS (SELECT client_id, SUM(amount) AS billed FROM invoices GROUP BY 1),
p AS (SELECT i.client_id, SUM(pay.amount) AS paid FROM payments pay JOIN invoices i ON i.id = pay.invoice_id GROUP BY 1)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(b.billed, 0) - COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS owed
FROM clients c LEFT JOIN b ON b.client_id = c.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.client_id = c.id
ORDER BY owed DESC;
Thoughts?

I'm a retired schoolteacher with an 8-inch telescope, and I posted this in my astronomy club's group: "Saturn tonight from the back garden. The rings were so sharp I could see the Cassini gap. I woke my wife to look. She said, 'It looks fake.' I said, 'That's the nicest thing anyone's said about it.'" Just a bit of fun, but I'd like your opinion.

Proposal to my team to kill our "smart suggestions" feature. Key paragraph: "Suggestions are used by 3% of users and generate 31% of our support tickets. Every feature is a promise to maintain it forever. We aren't deleting a feature; we're refusing a lifelong loan with a 3% return. Cut it, and move those two engineers to search, which 90% of users touch daily." Sending it Monday. Any thoughts first?

I'm 65 and just retired after 40 years as a high school band director. At my party I said: 'Forty years of teenagers, and I've heard every wrong note a human can play. I miss none of them. I miss all of them. Please don't clap on one and three. And if you must cry, do it in tempo.' Casually curious how that works on paper.

I'm a 34-year-old bus driver. I came up with Ramp Request. A rider at a stop opens the app and taps one button, "I need the ramp." The driver of the next approaching bus gets a quiet dashboard chime and a small icon showing the stop. Nobody has to wave or talk, and the driver can pull in at the right spot. I've pitched it to nobody yet. What's your take?

I'm a structural engineer. My app idea is CrackCheck. You put a printed 5 cm reference card next to a wall crack and photograph it. Computer vision measures the width to about 0.1 mm. Every month it reminds you to re-shoot from the same angle, using a ghost overlay of the last photo. If the width grows more than 0.3 mm, it tells you to call a professional. Thoughts?

I do alterations and slow-fashion tailoring, and I'm designing my logo. A yellow measuring tape curls into a spiral like a snail shell, its numbers getting smaller toward the middle. A small snail head and two feelers come out at the outer end. 'Slow Stitch' is stitched in dashes beneath it. I'm curious what you think.

I'm a chess club coach opening a quick takeaway cafe next to the park tables where people play. I'd like to name it "En Passant," the chess capture made in passing. Is the name clear and appealing to you? Be candid.

I'm a freelance-turned-staff designer and the rebrand has ballooned. Does this email to my manager work?
"Hi Jo, the rebrand has grown from 6 deliverables to 14 since kickoff. All reasonable asks, but at my pace it lands three weeks late. Options: cut the packaging mockups, bring in Rafi for 10 days, or move the deadline to 21 June. I lean toward Rafi. Which do you prefer?"

```python
import re
UNITS = {"h": 3600, "m": 60, "s": 1}
PART = r"(\d+)\s*([hms])"
def parse_duration(text):
    """'1h 30m' -> 5400"""
    if not re.search(PART, text) or re.sub(PART + r"|\s", "", text):
        raise ValueError(f"bad duration: {text!r}")
    return sum(int(n) * UNITS[u] for n, u in re.findall(PART, text))
```
</message>

units:
I'm a taxi driver, 40, and I moved here eleven years ago. I've been turning my feelings into songs. This is the chorus of the newest:
I wear two watches, one for here, one for home
One says it's noon, one says you're asleep
I live in the hours that don't have a name
Keeping time for the ones I can't keep
I'd be grateful for your opinion.

I'm a vet tech, and kids ask me about death all the time. Premise: Gus's goldfish dies, and at the funeral each relative gives a different eulogy. Gran's is wrong, Dad's is too short, and Gus slowly realizes each of them knew a different fish. Last line: "Gus said his own, and it was the longest." Could you give me your opinion?

I'm a second-year econ PhD student trying to write for a general audience. Title: "The Bus Fare Is a Lie We Agreed On." Opening: "Every city bus fare is a price set not by what a ride costs but by what a mayor can survive charging, which makes the fare box less a cash register than a weekly opinion poll." Does it work for you?

I'm a bike mechanic, and I want to open a repair cart outside the train station. You drop your bike at 8 a.m. with a tag that lists the issues, and I text you a quote before 9. If you reply "yes," it's done by 5:30, and you pick it up on your way home. If you reply "no," it's free of charge to wait. No shop rent, just a cart and a trailer. What do you think about this idea?

I taught high school English for 34 years and now I'm learning dessert. Lemon posset: simmer 2 cups heavy cream with ¾ cup sugar for 3 minutes, then whisk in ⅓ cup lemon juice and 1 tbsp olive oil. Pour into glasses and chill for 4 hours. Serve with rosemary shortbread. The olive oil makes it taste silky and slightly grassy. Would you like to tell me what you think?

Tonight I'm opening our astronomy club's star party. Here's the speech: "The light you'll see in Andromeda left 2.5 million years ago, before anything we'd call human. It has been traveling toward this field, this telescope, this paper cup of cocoa in your hand. Please don't rush. It's waited a long time for you. Red flashlights only, and be kind to the dark." What do you reckon?

I write narrative for video games and I'm trying prose for the first time. Here's an opening paragraph:
"The map was wrong in the way maps are wrong when they love you: it left out the cliff, the wolves, the long unfashionable middle of the journey, and drew the sea closer than it was. Imre followed it anyway. You can forgive a lot in something that wanted you to arrive."
How does it come across?

I'm a hobbyist drone photographer and want to pitch a hotel manager. Here's the email:
"Dear Ms. Aoki, I'm a local photographer, and last week at golden hour I shot your hotel's rooftop terrace from above, attached. The frame shows the pool, the hills behind, and the sunset hitting the cabanas. I'd be glad to shoot a full set of ten images for your website for $250. I'm licensed to fly in this area. May I send a quote? Regards, Daniel"
What do you think?

Here's the central question of my philosophy dissertation: "If moral testimony is epistemically legitimate in some domains, what explains why deferring to an expert about whether to donate seems acceptable while deferring about whether to forgive does not?" I'd appreciate your feedback.

I'm a night-shift nurse, eleven years in, and I've finally started writing. Here's a title and opening line for my first post: "What the Night Shift Knows About Silence." "At 3:40 a.m. the hospital hums in B-flat, and after eleven years I can tell from a change in that hum which floor is about to have a bad hour." I'd really appreciate your feedback.

I took one. It's in my tea. Thank you." Is it okay, or too sappy? I'm 67 and new to this.

I'm a vet tech, and kids ask me about death all the time. Premise: Gus's goldfish dies, and at the funeral each relative gives a different eulogy. Gran's is wrong, Dad's is too short, and Gus slowly realizes each of them knew a different fish. Last line: "Gus said his own, and it was the longest." Could you give me your opinion?

Accountant, 38, trying to switch into film production accounting. How's this paragraph? "I've audited a hospital, a shipping company, and a minor-league baseball team, and the most honest ledger belonged to the baseball team's snack stand. I like small chaos with receipts. Give me forty crew, cash per diems, and a location that changes on Thursday, and I'll hand you books that balance by Friday."

I'm a chef and I've been asked to speak at a food conference, which feels odd because I usually just cook. My opening: "Salt is the only rock we eat on purpose, and for ten thousand years we've argued about which ones taste best." What do you think?

I'm a plumber and I came up with this for the side of my van: "Every house has one pipe that's been quietly holding a grudge since 1974." My wife says it's too long for a van. Be straight with me: would you read it, and would you call me?

I'm a college student with dyslexia, and this is the app I wish existed. Point your camera at a printed page and it re-lays out the text live: wider spacing, a tinted band that follows your finger down one line at a time, and the rest of the page dimmed. No scanning, no PDF needed. Could you give me your thoughts on it?

I'm a retired electrician and this is my first poem since school. I wrote it about my mother's house:
I rewired my mother's house in 1987.
Behind the plaster, still, her wedding year:
cloth-wrapped cable, brittle as old licorice,
still carrying, without complaint,
the little the house had asked of it.
What would you say to it, honestly?

Just graduated and applying for backend jobs. This is the first bullet under my internship: "Reduced p95 checkout API latency from 1.8s to 310ms by replacing N+1 Postgres queries with batched lookups and adding a read-through Redis cache, saving an estimated $42K/yr in compute." What do you think? Anything you'd change?

I'm 72 and I've sewn for fifty years. My idea is adaptive clothing alterations. I'd convert people's own favorite shirts and trousers with magnetic buttons, side-opening seams and soft tags, for people with arthritis or limited mobility. My slogan is: "Keep the shirt you love. Change how it opens." I charge $18 per garment. I'm a little shy about putting this out there. Please tell me what you think.

units: I'm a nursing student and I blog about clinicals. Here's my latest title and first sentence: "What the Night Shift Taught Me Before I Had a License." "At 3 a.m. on my first rotation, a patient who hadn't spoken all week asked me to open the window, and I understood that half of nursing is noticing what people can't bring themselves to request." Thoughts? Anything you'd change?

I've been a landlord for 15 years, and I've seen too many deposit fights. My app idea is Day One. At move-in, tenant and landlord walk through together. The app guides them room by room, with a required photo of each wall, floor and appliance. Each photo is timestamped and cryptographically hashed. At the end, both sign and get the same PDF. Would tenants actually use this? What do you think?

I'm 74, a retired welder, and I've been playing blues guitar since Nixon. Wrote this one after my wife passed. The chorus goes:
Woke up this morning, coffee already made
Ruthie's been gone three years, but the timer don't know
So I pour her a cup and I drink mine slow
Lord, that's how a love goes on, even after you go
Tell me what you hear in it.

I'm 80 and my granddaughter said I should show someone. It's a story from my childhood, dressed up a bit:
"The summer I was nine, the circus came to Ballina and left without its elephant. Nobody could explain it. She stood in Mr. Doyle's field for six weeks, enormous and patient, eating his hay, until the whole parish had told her something it had never told another living soul."
What do you think, dear?

I volunteer in a hospice kitchen. Our residents often want something gentle, so I made this ginger chicken congee. Simmer 1 cup jasmine rice in 8 cups chicken stock with 5 thick slices of ginger and a bone-in thigh for 90 minutes. Shred the chicken and stir it back in. Top with scallion, a drizzle of toasted sesame oil, and a little white pepper. Honest opinion welcome.

I run a coffee cart near the train station. This one's about a regular. Any thoughts would be great:
The first customer is always the widower.
He orders two cups
and drinks the one that's his
slowly,
so the other can stay warm.

I'm launching a green burial company called Return. The symbol is a single leaf, outlined, whose veins branch out in the closed concentric whorls of a fingerprint, so the leaf also reads as a human thumbprint. Deep moss green, slightly uneven line, like it was pressed in ink. Name below in a quiet serif. I'm hoping you can give me an honest response.

Long-time fantasy reader, first-time writer here. My novel begins: "Tuesday was the day Thornwick hid its children, so the dragon's tax collector found only goats, a very old man, and an unusually loud silence." Would you tell me what you think? Be gentle, I'm a bit anxious about this.

I'm a club chess player, 52, and I blog about my games. This one's titled "I Lost to an Eight-Year-Old and Here's the Move That Did It." It begins: "She pushed her h-pawn on move six, I laughed, and for the next forty minutes I learned that being amused is the most expensive mistake in chess." Honest feedback welcome!

I'm a marine biologist and I'm starting a company called Shell Game. We pick up oyster shells from restaurants weekly, a fee of $30 a month, cure them for six months and deliver them to reef restoration projects. Each restaurant receives a plaque: "Your shells built 3 square feet of reef." Photos and GPS coordinates are included each quarter. Would restaurants actually pay? Curious what you think.

units: Hi! For my nursing capstone I came up with this: "Among night-shift nurses on medical-surgical wards, does a protected 20-minute nap during breaks reduce medication administration errors in the final three hours of shift compared with caffeine alone?" I'm a bit nervous about showing my advisor. Thoughts?

I'm 22, bilingual, and I wrote this chorus about my mom making tortillas before work:
Mi mamá cuenta el mundo en tortillas
One for the rent, one for the rain
Dos para mí, y una para la esperanza
Flip it quick before it burns again
I'd really like to know what you think, especially about mixing the languages.

Firefighter, 33. Wrote this on shift, be straight with me: "I run toward things for a living, which is why I'm slow to say what I feel. I make a decent chili. I fall asleep during every movie by minute forty. I'll carry your couch up four flights and never mention it. Looking for someone who texts back when I'm off and understands when I can't."

As a new mom going back to school, I'm writing about lullabies. My thesis: "Lullabies across cultures are strikingly dark, with falling cradles and wolves at the door, because they soothe not through content but by letting the parent perform her own anxiety for the infant in a safe, rhythmic, controlled form." I'd love to hear what you think.

I'm a vet tech and my colleagues keep telling me to write down the stuff I say. This one came up on Tuesday: "Every vet knows the animal is rarely the one who needs sedating." I'd love to hear what someone outside the clinic thinks.
I'm 10 and I made up a joke for my class talent show. What did the clock say when it got sent to the principal? "I was only tocking." My mum says I should ask someone else. What do you think?

I'm putting this on the counter card at my bakery to get people to bring their own boxes: "Our croissants take three days to make. Their box takes three seconds to throw away. Bring your own container and we'll take 50 cents off, because anything worth waiting for deserves better than cardboard." Would this make you do it? Be blunt.
For my marketing class I invented an alarm clock that wakes you with gradual sunlight. My slogan is "Sunrise, minus the rooster." Can you give me feedback? My professor wants peer opinions.

Retired baker, still experimenting. Rye and caraway sourdough discard crackers: 150g discard, 60g rye flour, 40g olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp caraway seeds. Mix, rest 30 minutes, roll paper thin, brush with water, and sprinkle with flaky salt and more seeds. Bake at 180°C for 18 minutes, rotating once, until they're deep amber and snap. I'd like a second opinion, please.

I'm a 34-year-old home inspector, and I've been writing a horror screenplay on the side. Here's the logline: "A home inspector notices that every house in a new subdivision has one more room on the inside than on the outside, and the extra rooms are starting to be occupied." Be honest, what's your take?

Sixteen summers later, forty families eat from it. The water main beneath it is failing, and replacing it costs $11,200. We're asking you to help keep the tomatoes coming." Thoughts?

I'm a grad student who writes songs to cope with deadlines. This chorus is about my grandfather's radio, which I still keep on my desk. Does it work as a chorus, in your view?
He tuned it by feel, a quarter inch of static,
found the ballgame in the hiss like a man finding a door.
Now it sits on my desk, picking up nothing,
but I turn the dial anyway. I just want to hear it once more.

I'm a hospice night nurse, 43, and my coworkers encouraged me to write this down: "When a hospice nurse notices her dying patients all ask for the same stranger in their final hour, she tracks him down and finds a lonely locksmith who has never met any of them." Tell me what you think, please.

I translate Korean webtoons as a fan hobby, and I'm applying for a junior localization job. This is my cover letter paragraph on translation philosophy. What do you make of it?
"In one series, a character says '밥 먹었어?' to mean 'I love you.' A literal translation says 'Did you eat?' A faithful one says something else entirely. I've learned to keep the question and add the worry around it: 'Have you eaten yet? You look tired.'"

I'd love a second pair of eyes on this bullet: "Built a privilege-log template and tagging protocol that cut document review for a 400,000-page antitrust production from an estimated 9 weeks to 5, with zero clawback requests." appear, stop again
thoughts?

Here's my one sentence: "Universities auction off decommissioned lab equipment for pennies, so we recondition and calibrate it, certify it, and sell forty-year-old spectrometers to high school and community college labs at a tenth of the price of new." I'm 71 and I knit blankets to sell at the craft fair. My granddaughter told me to ask people online for opinions. This is my tag:
"Merino cot blanket, knitted in honeycomb stitch, which holds warmth without weight. Washed in lanolin so it stays soft. Nine evenings of work. Machine washable on the wool cycle, and made to be handed down: the edges are bound twice, because babies are hard on everything."
Does it work?

I run a small lawn-care company and I'm applying for a small-business loan, so I'm rewriting my bio into resume form. Here's the main bullet: "Grew a one-truck lawn-care business to $186K annual revenue in three years; converted 70% of customers to seasonal contracts by texting before-and-after photos after every visit." What's your reaction?

Our daughter cried when the snow melted, so I wrote this on my lunch breaks. "Snowman, Stored." Odile hides her snowman in the chest freezer between the peas and Dad's fish, visiting daily with a scarf. By July he's the size of a grapefruit. In December she introduces him to the first snowfall like a returning relative. I'm a plumber, not an author. Thoughts?

Hi! I play chess competitively as a hobby, and I'm toasting two fellow club members. Here goes: "In chess, we say the opening is theory, the middlegame is imagination, and the endgame is technique. Raj and Claire skipped the opening, played a wildly imaginative middlegame in the club parking lot, and now they're in an endgame where the only rule is that nobody resigns. May every draw be by agreement. To Raj and Claire." Thoughts?

I'm 40 and have never lifted before, so I kept it simple. Mon/Wed/Fri: goblet squat, dumbbell bench, one-arm row, Romanian deadlift, plank, always in that order. Start at 3x8, add one rep per week until 3x12, then add weight. Tue/Thu: 20-minute walk. Sat: something fun. Sun: rest. I write down how I felt after each session. I'm a bit nervous about sharing it. What do you think?

"My grandmother runs a four-person courier service and tracked deliveries in a spiral notebook. I built her a small app that texts customers when a driver is ten minutes away. the soft one, the sideways one,
the one that means you're late, come in.

I'm a 45-year-old accountant who just started a punk band with two friends from the office. Our chorus:
I carry the one, I carry the two
Carry your lunch order, carry the blame
Tonight I'm carrying nothing but a guitar
And my own goddamn name
What's your take? Please be straight with me.

First-year law student. I told my study group: "The 'reasonable person' is the only one in law school who's never late, never confused, and has always done the reading." Everyone groaned in a good way, I think. What do you make of it?

I garden on an allotment and wrote this to decide whether to water, with recent rain counting for more. Rough hobby code, but I'd like an opinion:
```python
def needs_water(rain_mm, threshold=15, decay=0.7):
    """rain_mm is oldest-first, one value per day."""
    effective = sum(mm * decay**age
                    for age, mm in enumerate(reversed(rain_mm)))
    return effective < threshold
```

Flattening JSON order items in Postgres. Our orders come from three vendors, so the key isn't always present:
SELECT o.id, item->>'sku' AS sku, (item->>'qty')::int AS qty
FROM orders o
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(o.payload->'items') AS item
WHERE o.payload ? 'items';
Backend dev, 2 years of experience. I'd like your thoughts, especially on whether I'm missing something.

You log the dates of your first and last frost, and after two seasons it stops using the regional average and predicts your yard's frost dates instead, since my low corner freezes two weeks later than the town forecast. units: I'm a finish carpenter applying for a set builder job at a theater. Wrote this: "Furniture is built to last fifty years. A set is built to look like it will, for six weeks, and then be burned. I find that freeing. I can fake a hundred-year-old oak door from luan and one can of walnut stain, and I can make it survive a slammed exit every night." Does that work, do you think?

I moved here from Busan eight months ago and I'm writing in English to practice. I wrote this haiku:
Snow in a new town—
I practice my name aloud
until it sounds mine
Please tell me what you think, and about my English too.

I'm a 62-year-old dairy farmer. At my neighbor Walt's retirement, I said: 'Walt farmed the same hundred and sixty acres as his father. People call that standing still. But I watched him walk that fence line every morning for forty years, and the ground under him changed more than any of us did. You don't stay in one place by not moving. You stay by tending.' Honest feedback welcome.

Hey, I'm a 45-year-old pediatric nurse, and I wrote this for a short film contest: "When a ten-year-old's imaginary friend begins aging faster than she does, she has one childhood left to keep him alive." Does it work as a logline? Any feedback welcome.

I farm a few acres and write stories in the winter. Here's the beginning of one, if you'd give me your honest reaction: "Ma used to say the wind in Dry Fork had opinions. The morning it started whispering our names one by one, I figured it had finally made up its mind about us. Pa ignored it. Pa had ignored most things, including the well, which had been dry since March and had the manners to be quiet about it."

I make kombucha to sell at the farmers' market, and I'm designing a project about its pH during fermentation. I'll brew five identical 1 L jars, and test pH with a calibrated meter every 12 hours for 14 days. I'll also record the temperature, and taste-test safely only after day 7. The graph should show when it crosses pH 3.5. What would you say about the design?

I'm an occupational therapist, and this is my layout for a sensory garden in a dementia care home. A looped path, 1.5m wide, with no dead ends, so no one gets stuck. Along it, five stations: scent (lavender, rosemary), touch (lamb's ear, grasses), sound (bamboo, wind chimes), taste (raspberries, mint) and a familiar-memory corner with a washing line and a shed. Handrails run along the edges, and the seating is every 12m. Would you give me your thoughts?

After 30 years as a newspaper reporter, I'm opening a cafe in the old Gazette building, and I'm calling it "Stop Press." The menu will be printed on broadsheet and the coffee will be strong enough to meet a deadline. Does the name have the right ring to it? Tell me straight, I've had worse feedback from editors.
